name: Erik Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager on a dairy farm, 220 cows, milked twice a day. First milking starts at half four, so I'm up at four. Milking takes about two and a half hours with me and one other in the parlour, then it's feeding, checking for lame cows, the calves, and whatever's broken. Second milking's at half three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The routine. Cows like routine and so do I. I know which cow comes in first every morning, number 114, the same old girl for six years. There's something in that, knowing what's coming.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hours, and the pay for those hours. I'm good at this, I won a herd health award at the county show last year, but the farm pays what it can, and that isn't much. Anna, my girlfriend, works on reception at the vet practice. Between us we've got maybe three weeks of savings. The car's held together with hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't matter to me either way. I don't use it, I don't need it. Cows don't care about search engines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the same thing. My problem is the milk price. The dairy pays what it pays, and it goes up and down, and my boss, Mr Hollis, can't promise a rise till it's steady. AI doesn't come into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep milking, keep my head down, ask for a rise when the milk price is up again. I'd maybe put a bit more aside if the car lasts another winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to feel, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for the milk price swinging around?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of everyone. Supermarkets, the dairies, weather, the world price. I don't think there's one villain. People who say there is usually want your vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone tried to get you to use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna's tried. She showed me how to ask one about treating mastitis, that's an udder infection. It gave a decent answer, I'll admit. But I'd still ring the vet, because the vet's seen our herd and the computer hasn't.

S0.say: I'd say it doesn't matter to me either way. I don't use AI, I don't need it, and cows don't care about search engines.
S0.think: My real problem is the milk price, which goes up and down so my boss can't promise a rise. AI doesn't come into it.
S0.do: Keeps milking, keeps his head down and asks for a rise when the milk price recovers. Puts a bit more aside if the car lasts another winter.
S0.feel: Calm; there's nothing here to feel strongly about.
S0.quote: I'd still ring the vet, because the vet's seen our herd and the computer hasn't.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is quiet, steady and plain-spoken. He refuses to blame any single villain for the milk price, which fits his middle-ground outlook. He admits the AI gave a decent answer but still won't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's how it always goes. Things change slowly and people adjust. I wouldn't post about it. I don't post about anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly fine for me, but the fewer beginners bit worries me a bit. Dairy can't find young people already. If the colleges and agencies cut back, Mr Hollis will be even shorter of hands, and it's me who covers the gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to hang on to the relief milker we have, Sasha, by putting in a word for a small rise for her. I'd write down how I do things, the routines, the cows to watch, in a notebook, in case someone new comes in and needs to learn fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Mostly tired, thinking about covering more shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A notebook rather than anything on a computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notebook. The blue one in the parlour office. I've already got a page on each problem cow. If a new lad comes, he can read it in the tea break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many shifts do you cover now when someone's off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter, I did eleven days straight in February when Sasha had flu. Anna said I smelled of the parlour in my sleep. I said that's the smell of wages.

S1.say: I'd say that's how things always go: they change slowly and people adjust. I wouldn't post about it, because I don't post about anything.
S1.think: It's mostly fine for me, but fewer beginners worries me because dairy is already short of young people. If the colleges cut back, I'm the one who covers the gaps.
S1.do: Puts in a word for a small rise to keep the relief milker. Writes his routines and notes on problem cows in a notebook so a new worker could learn fast.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, and mostly tired at the thought of covering more shifts.
S1.quote: Anna said I smelled of the parlour in my sleep. I said that's the smell of wages.
S1.fieldNote: His worry is practical: fewer young workers means more shifts for him. The blue notebook is his version of a system, firmly on paper. There's dry humour under the plain manner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's rough for office people and something should be done, but I'd want to see what before I agreed with anyone. Both sides would be shouting, and both would be half right. I'd keep out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about Anna. A vet practice reception is exactly the kind of office job those assistants could do: bookings, reminders, bills. If she lost her job, we'd be on my wage alone, and that's not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Anna to start looking early, maybe at something hands-on, like the vet nurse training, if the practice would help pay. We'd stop eating out entirely, which isn't much of a cut because we hardly do. I'd ask Mr Hollis about overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not my job on the line, but it's our money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Anna the evening it became real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much the first evening. I'd make her tea and let her be angry. Then a day or two later I'd sit down with the bank statements and we'd work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd you be angry at, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. The company that sold the practice the system, maybe. But the practice owner's got bills too. I'd be angry at the situation more than any person.

S2.say: I'd say it's rough for office people and something should be done, but I'd want to see what before agreeing with anyone. Both sides would be half right, and I'd keep out of it.
S2.think: I'd worry about Anna, because reception work at the vet practice is exactly what these assistants could take over. On my wage alone, we wouldn't manage.
S2.do: Encourages his partner to look early at hands-on work such as vet nurse training, ideally paid for by the practice. Cuts the little they spend on eating out and asks his boss about overtime.
S2.feel: Anxious, because even though his job is safe, their household income isn't.
S2.quote: I'd make her tea and let her be angry. Then a day or two later I'd sit down with the bank statements and we'd work it out.
S2.fieldNote: The threat reaches him through his partner's office job, and his mood moves up sharply because of their thin savings. He won't pick a political side or a villain. He shows care in very practical ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and the government should sort out who gets what, fairly, without wrecking the economy. That's about as political as I get. I'd vote, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fairly safe, the cows still need milking. But house prices booming means we'll never buy, and Mr Hollis might sell up if the land's suddenly worth a fortune. If he sells to someone who wants a horse paddock, I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hollis honestly about his plans, which would be awkward because he's a private man. I'd keep my head down and work harder so I'm the one any new owner wants to keep. And I'd look at herd manager jobs further afield, just to know what's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The job's fine until it isn't, and I wouldn't get much warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd look further afield. Would you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to. Anna's family's here, and I like knowing the roads. But if it was move or nothing, I'd move. I'd just complain the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work harder. Can you work harder than four in the morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. Not longer. Better, maybe. Get the cell count down, that's how the dairy measures udder health, keep the cows sound, so the numbers speak for me if anyone new is looking.

S3.say: I'd say it's a mess and the government should sort out who gets what fairly, without wrecking the economy. I'd vote, and that's as political as I get.
S3.think: I'm fairly safe, because the cows still need milking. But booming land prices might tempt my boss to sell, and if the buyer wants a horse paddock, I'm out.
S3.do: Asks his boss about his plans despite the awkwardness. Works on herd health figures such as the cell count, a measure of udder health, so his record speaks for him, and checks herd manager jobs further away.
S3.feel: Anxious, because the job is fine until it suddenly isn't.
S3.quote: I'd hate to. Anna's family's here, and I like knowing the roads.
S3.fieldNote: His fear moves from his partner's job to the land itself being sold. When I asked, he accepted he can't work longer, only better. Moving away is a last resort, held up by family and familiarity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the card. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in dairy aren't new, and they're not as clever as the adverts. I'd say it calmly, because people would be panicking. But I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I know what it means. Mr Hollis already had a quote for robot milkers two years ago. He said no because of the cost. If robots get cheaper and smarter, he'd say yes, and a robot dairy needs one person watching a laptop, not me in a parlour. I've never touched a laptop for work in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask straight out whether he's buying them. If he is, I'd ask to stay on for the cows' health, the feet, the calving, the things the robot can't do. If he says no, I'd look for a farm that still milks the old way, even if it's miles away. There'll be fewer each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like watching weather come over the hill and knowing your hay's still out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the laptop side yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could try. I don't think I'd be good at it, and I don't think I'd enjoy it. I'd rather be in with the cows. Maybe that's stubborn. Anna would say it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first bill that goes unpaid if your wage stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the car loan, and then we're stuck, because there's no bus out here. That's the bit that frightens me. No car, no job, no way to get to a job.

S4.say: I'd say dairy robots aren't new and aren't as clever as the adverts. I'd say it calmly, because other people would be panicking.
S4.think: My boss already had a quote for robot milkers two years ago and only said no because of the cost. A robot dairy needs one person at a laptop, not me in a parlour.
S4.do: Asks his boss directly whether he's buying robots and offers to stay on for herd health, feet and calving. If that fails, looks for farms still milking the old way, even far away.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like seeing a storm coming while the hay is still out.
S4.quote: It's like watching weather come over the hill and knowing your hay's still out.
S4.fieldNote: This is the one scenario that is concrete for him, because his boss has already priced robot milkers. He calls himself stubborn rather than learn the laptop side. The car loan is his weak point: without it he can't get to any job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because Mr Hollis has already looked at them. What would help is time. A year's notice, some redundancy pay that means something, and maybe a bus out here so losing the car isn't losing everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the cows. A robot milks a cow, fine. But who notices 114's limping before it's bad? Somebody's got to still know the herd.

headlineQuote: No car, no job, no way to get to a job.
portrait: Erik Gupta is 27 and manages a 220-cow dairy herd, up at four for milking, living with his girlfriend Anna, who works on reception at a vet practice. He's quiet, dryly funny and fond of routine, keeps his notes in a blue notebook and won't use AI even when it gives a decent answer. He refuses to blame any single villain or pick a political side. Through the middle scenarios his worry is Anna's office job and the farm being sold, and in the robot scenario his boss's old quote for robot milkers makes the threat very real. He'd rather stay with the cows than learn the laptop side, and his weak point is the car he needs to reach any job.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because his boss has already priced robot milkers and would only need someone at a laptop.
whatWouldHelp: Time: a year's notice, redundancy pay that means something, and a bus out to the farm so losing the car doesn't mean losing everything.
